kp.k: Equitable legal AI requires calibration and regulatory reform
kp.d: Simshaw presents a normative framework, rather than an original empirical evaluation, arguing that AI's contribution to access to justice depends on stakeholders' ability to design appropriate services. He recommends regulatory reforms enabling competition and collaboration between legal professionals and technologists, while protecting consumers. The article addresses both legal technology generally and its increasingly AI-driven forms.
qs: Therefore, calibration is not about maximizing AI use. Rather, it is about making more informed decisions about what AI should, and should not, be used for.
Legal AI does not have to be a “necessary evil” for licensed legal professionals or “better than nothing” for consumers.

kp.k: The justice gap extends beyond unaffordable lawyers
kp.d: The article reports that in 2017 only fourteen percent of low-income Americans received adequate legal attention to their reported problems, citing the Legal Services Corporation. It also cites a 2021 nationwide survey identifying 10,479 civil legal aid attorneys, just over one per 10,000 people below 200% of the federal poverty level. Simshaw identifies additional barriers including limited legal awareness, language, geography, educational resources, and distrust, and describes COVID-19 as exacerbating unmet need.
qs: In 2017, only fourteen percent of low-income Americans received adequate legal attention to the legal problems they reported.

In 2021, a nationwide survey found that there were only 10,479 civil legal aid attorneys in the U.S., equaling just over one for every 10,000 people whose incomes fall below 200% of the federal poverty level.
But cost is far from the only barrier, and assuming that it is risks underestimating the myriad social disparities that keep legal services elusive for many groups.

kp.k: Automation can expand assistance across service settings
kp.d: Drawing on existing scholarship and practitioner accounts, Simshaw describes guided interviews, automated documents, intake classifiers, legal research, e-discovery, and litigation analytics. These can support self-help, legal aid, limited-license professionals, and law firms. Potential benefits include identifying legal problems, connecting consumers to professionals, and freeing providers for human and creative work; the article does not establish that all such tools achieve these benefits.
qs: By simplifying these processes, these services help bring individuals into the legal problem-solving landscape who might otherwise have been left out.

If AI and machine learning can appropriately complete or assist with once-time-consuming tasks, lawyers and other providers can spend less time on the mechanical aspects of legal problem solving and more time on the human and creative aspects.

kp.k: Efficiency could support flat fees and broader markets
kp.d: The article describes a possible shift from bespoke delivery toward disaggregated and commodified legal work. Drawing on Kristen Sonday's account of document automation, it explains how fewer lawyer-hours can support affordable flat-fee options. Wider access, higher matter volumes, and greater competition are presented as potential consequences, conditional on diverse providers being able to harness the technology effectively.
qs: The time and cost savings from these efficiencies can be passed on to consumers in the form of increased flat-fee service options, as opposed to hourly billing.
But these optimistic prognostications for an efficient, accessible AI-driven legal problem-solving landscape presume that a wide range of stakeholders will be able to effectively harness AI.

kp.k: Inferior automated assistance could entrench unequal justice
kp.d: The first scenario Simshaw synthesizes from the literature is that poorer consumers receive inferior technology-driven assistance while wealthier clients retain superior human representation. He reports concerns about predatory services, consumers' inability to detect harm, automated triage relegating people to self-help, and technological provision weakening support for full-service legal aid. This is a risk scenario, not a demonstrated inevitable outcome.
qs: The first two-tiered system concern reflects fear that technology-driven legal solutions will be accepted—or worse, expected—as the predominant source of legal assistance for those who cannot afford what are assumed to be superior human-driven legal services.
Moreover, an inaccurate perception of the effectiveness of AI-driven services could lead to the further abandonment of more traditional human-centered legal aid solutions to the justice gap.

kp.k: Superior AI augmentation could concentrate provider advantage
kp.d: The second scenario reverses the assumed quality hierarchy: well-resourced firms could combine lawyers and AI to outperform providers lacking capital, technical staff, tailored tools, data, and cross-industry relationships. Simshaw warns that expanded capacity at corporate-oriented firms need not address underserved populations' different legal needs. He attributes claims of inevitable superiority of AI-augmented lawyers to other commentators rather than presenting them as established findings.
qs: A second two-tiered scenario is rooted in greater faith in the potential power of legal AI, but fears that the power will not be evenly distributed throughout the landscape, to the ultimate detriment of consumers.
The economic and human resources available to wealthier providers make them better able to tailor their technology to their specific needs, which historically have been serving corporate clients.

kp.k: AI could leave existing exclusion largely unchanged
kp.d: The third scenario is continued separation between people who can and cannot obtain legal assistance. Simshaw reports arguments that technical underperformance, slow development, uncertain returns, professional conservatism, and startups' changing commercial priorities could prevent meaningful improvement. He explicitly treats the three scenarios as contingent and potentially overlapping.
qs: This scenario would ultimately result in a failure to significantly alter the landscape and a perpetuation of the unacceptable justice-gap status quo.
None of these scenarios is inevitable, and it is possible that the future is one in which parts of all three scenarios are realized.

kp.k: Consumer-centered design must address exclusion and cultural differences
kp.d: Calibration must consider legal awareness, technological confidence, literacy, affordability, connectivity, language, and cultural communication practices. Simshaw describes matching machine-learning classifiers to consumers' everyday descriptions, including the Learned Hands crowdsourcing example. He advocates diverse design teams, cultural-competence expertise and training, and retaining face-to-face routes where appropriate; access to a device alone does not establish meaningful access.
qs: Just because AI might open some “virtual doors” for some consumers does not mean that all consumers will be willing or able to walk through them.
Because consumers often do not know the legal terms corresponding to their issues, it is essential that the “classifiers” coded into the AI match the consumers’ understanding of their issues.
Effectively calibrated legal AI also requires culturally competent design, which is an inextricable prerequisite for access to justice efforts.

kp.k: Legal issues require different levels of human involvement
kp.d: Simshaw distinguishes relatively simple, bounded matters potentially suitable for automated self-help from high-stakes, individualized, emotionally consequential, or complex matters requiring substantial professional involvement. Examples include uncontested divorces and parking fines versus matters involving life and liberty or risky business transactions. Tools should identify vulnerability and route consumers to professionals. He also warns that missing digitized records, illustrated by heirs' property, can exclude marginalized communities from data-driven services.
qs: Stakeholders must also consider what degree of AI reliance or restraint is appropriate given the nature of the legal issues at play.

AI-driven tools that rely on digitized records would either be ineffective for such practice areas and communities or fail to account for important non-digitized information that is central to their legal issues.
In these cases, the nature of the legal issues might be such that the professional should be more prominently involved, exercising AI restraint by only relying on AI for limited tasks, or not at all.

kp.k: Task suitability favors augmentation over autonomous legal judgment
kp.d: The article cites literature reporting superior accuracy and speed for e-discovery and some language-processing tasks, but distinguishes these from strategic decisions, factual investigation, persuasion, and individualized legal writing. In its 2022 framing, AI should inform rather than automate major case decisions. Simshaw links human involvement to supervision obligations and notes the ABA's 2012 change of Model Rule 5.3's title from nonlawyer 'Assistants' to 'Assistance,' encompassing technological services more broadly.
qs: But not all tasks are equally suited for the same level of AI reliance.
For decisions such as where to file a lawsuit, what claims to bring, and what strategy to employ, AI in the near term is likely to only be effective to inform, not to automate, the decision.
Such decisions have a serious impact on a client’s case and should require human judgment, or at least human confirmation, that the decision is the prudent one.

kp.k: Client-facing automation introduces communication and ethical risks
kp.d: Simshaw identifies risks where chatbots cannot establish whether consumers understand legal information, educate them appropriately, or identify conflicts before collecting sensitive facts. Consumers may disclose too little or too much. He specifically reports Amy Cyphert's warning against using then-current GPT-3 for real-time legal chatbots because training data can generate biased or racist outputs; this is a historically situated concern, not a finding about all subsequent models.
qs: Until AI can reliably identify and respond to such situations, processes such as client intake using tools like chatbots could result in myriad ethical issues.

Similarly, a lawyer might be more likely to quickly identify a conflict of interest during intake and be able to end the communication promptly, whereas a chatbot might continue to amass information that the firm would rather not possess.
“should not be used in its current state to power real-time legal ‘chatbots’ on client-facing websites.”

kp.k: Bias and opacity require deliberate design safeguards
kp.d: The article explains how designers' judgments, homogeneous teams, biased historical data, and absent machine-readable records can reproduce or amplify inequality. Conversely, drawing on McPeak, it identifies potential for AI to reveal improper decision factors. Simshaw recommends transparency, diverse expertise, scrutiny of data and algorithms, and reviewable coding decisions; these are proposed safeguards rather than demonstrated guarantees of fairness.
qs: Bias can manifest in virtually any AI-driven legal process.
Whether AI combats or amplifies bias depends on how effectively the underlying processes have been calibrated.
Finally, process calibration must ensure sufficient transparency into how AI is performing or assisting with each process.
Black boxes also make bias harder to detect.

kp.k: Resources and resilience constrain effective AI adoption
kp.d: Simshaw distinguishes acquisition costs from the expense of design, testing, maintenance, infrastructure, data conversion, and computational capacity. Small firms and legal aid organizations face particular constraints, while established large firms can face costly legacy-system replacement. Resilience additionally requires leadership, algorithmic literacy, training, time for trial and error, and tolerance of uncertainty; ethical anxiety and lack of financial or peer safety nets can inhibit experimentation.
qs: While resources are necessary for legal AI calibration, they are not sufficient.
Designers and users of legal AI must also be resilient in order to adapt and respond to inevitable calibration challenges.
Resilience during calibration also requires ample amounts of one of AI’s most important ingredients: time.
Given the significant amount of capital needed to acquire, support, and sustain data-driven technologies, even large law firms may need outside investment.

kp.k: Cross-disciplinary relationships face ownership and UPL barriers
kp.d: Effective calibration requires reciprocal advice: lawyers need technical expertise, while technologists need legal and contextual knowledge. Simshaw argues that restrictions on nonlawyer ownership and investment, modeled on ABA rules and adopted by jurisdictions, limit financing and enduring partnerships. Varied and uncertain unauthorized-practice-of-law definitions may deter collaboration even absent an actual violation. He recommends clearer boundaries, including for informational and scrivener services.
qs: Calibration requires relationships where expertise is shared in both directions.

Short of actual violations, confusion over the application of UPL definitions to software and online services could be enough to scare off potential investors and collaborators, stunting innovative access to justice efforts.

Concerns about engaging in UPL could be alleviated by clearer definitions of the “practice of law” across jurisdictions, which would provide technologists, legal service providers, and other stakeholders with the comfort and stability necessary to innovate

kp.k: Competition and transparency should accompany regulatory innovation
kp.d: Simshaw acknowledges that consolidation can fund research and make integrated AI services cheaper, but reports concerns that incumbent control of data, computing, and scarce talent can suppress wider innovation or displace access-to-justice priorities. He recommends enabling more diverse providers to compete. For services outside practice-of-law regulation, proposed protections include public accuracy rates, evaluations of consumer experiences and outcomes, certifications, and general consumer-protection enforcement.
qs: Competition in legal AI development will help ensure that the market is providing effectively-tailored services for currently underserved legal service providers and consumers.
To promote both competition and calibration, technological innovation should be accompanied by regulatory innovation.
Similarly, evaluations could track results and consumer experiences, providing helpful data to consumers and innovators alike.

kp.k: Regulatory sandboxes enable supervised experimentation and evidence gathering
kp.d: Simshaw favors monitored experimentation over immediately removing restrictions wholesale. He reports that Utah launched the first U.S. legal-services regulatory sandbox in 2020 and extended its duration from two to seven years in May 2021, while Arizona eliminated its ownership and investment restriction without experimentation. Proposed sandbox uses include equity partnerships between small firms and AI experts, and limited UPL exceptions. Reporting and oversight would support decisions about permanent authorization, rule changes, consumer protection, and possible cross-jurisdictional reciprocity.
qs: After successful operation in the sandbox and the production of relevant data, regulators can decide whether to approve the service for longer-term operation or amend certain rules to allow it and similar services to enter the market.
Utah launched the U.S.’s first regulatory sandbox for legal services in 2020, and in May 2021 extended its duration from two to seven years.
For example, a small law firm could propose to offer a small percentage of ownership in the firm to an AI expert who the firm might not otherwise have been able to afford to hire.
The potential benefits of regulatory sandboxes with regard to legal AI go far beyond the issue of firm ownership.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Simshaw argues that AI can expand legal assistance and improve lawyers’ productivity, but its access-to-justice benefits depend on equitable access and context-sensitive design rather than adoption alone.
pts.d: The article identifies potential benefits from automated intake, issue identification, document generation, legal research, discovery, and litigation analytics. These can support self-help, connect consumers to professionals, reduce mechanical work, and enable lower-cost or flat-fee services. Simshaw also synthesizes three possible inequitable outcomes: poorer consumers receive inferior automated assistance while wealthier consumers retain human lawyers; well-resourced firms combine lawyers and AI to outperform less-resourced providers; or AI fails to overcome the existing divide between those who can obtain legal help and those who cannot. These are conditional scenarios, not findings that any one outcome is inevitable. His proposed response is 'calibration': designing the appropriate balance of human and AI involvement around consumers, legal issues, and processes. He argues that shortages of resources, resilience, and cross-industry relationships impede that design. AI-market consolidation can compound these barriers. Clarifying unauthorized-practice rules and experimenting with ownership and investment reforms through supervised regulatory sandboxes could facilitate collaboration, generate evidence, and expand access while protecting consumers.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article offers a literature-based legal and policy argument, supported by cited statistics, technology examples, professional rules, and emerging regulatory initiatives—not an original empirical test of AI’s effects on access to justice.
pts.d: For the baseline justice gap, Simshaw cites the Legal Services Corporation’s 2017 finding that only 14% of low-income Americans received adequate attention for reported legal problems and a 2021 national survey identifying 10,479 civil legal aid attorneys. These establish unmet need, not AI effectiveness. For efficiency and accuracy, he relies on published accounts of technology-assisted review, including cited reports of a 75% reduction in discovery time and superior accuracy and recall relative to human review; these are task-specific secondary evidence, not general performance measurements for legal AI. Operational illustrations include legal-aid intake classifiers, automated forms, and Learned Hands’ crowdsourced labeling of lay legal questions. Risks are supported by literature on digital exclusion, consumer difficulties identifying reliable online legal services, algorithmic bias, and absent digitized records in heirs’ property matters. He cites GPT-3 research to illustrate chatbot risks. Regulatory evidence includes Utah’s sandbox launched in 2020 and extended in 2021, and Arizona’s removal of its ownership restriction. The proposed benefits of broader sandbox adoption and cross-industry ownership arrangements remain argued mechanisms and hypothetical applications, rather than measured outcomes. Predictions cited from other scholars are supporting literature, not interviews or independent findings generated by Simshaw.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2022 article distinguishes existing narrow applications from conditional future expansion; it provides no fixed date for profession-wide transformation or closure of the justice gap.
pts.d: Simshaw describes discovery, research, intake, and document automation as existing or emerging applications at publication. His broader claims concern the years ahead and depend on effective design, suitable data, infrastructure, affordability, user accessibility, professional oversight, and regulatory change. He expects near-term AI to inform rather than autonomously make consequential strategic decisions. Greater automation may be suitable for straightforward, limited-outcome matters, while complex, high-stakes, emotionally significant, or poorly digitized matters warrant greater human involvement. Consumer literacy, language, cultural communication patterns, broadband access, and capacity to recognize legal needs qualify assumptions about self-help uptake. Bias control and transparency are further conditions. Development requires sustained trial and error, not merely an initial software purchase. The article discusses a possible future professional obligation to use demonstrably effective, broadly adopted AI, drawing on cited legal-ethics commentary; it does not establish a universal present requirement to use all AI tools. Its technical expectations, including limitations on persuasive writing and autonomous legal analysis, reflect the publication’s historical context.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Effects differ across underserved consumers, small providers, large firms, technologists, and the broader public; productivity gains for wealthy clients do not automatically close the justice gap.
pts.d: Low- and middle-income individuals, self-represented litigants, rural residents, immigrants, people with limited English proficiency, and digitally excluded communities may gain affordable information and assistance, but may also face inferior service, inaccessible interfaces, biased outputs, or reduced human assistance. Small businesses, nonprofits, and community organizations could gain transactional support. Legal-aid organizations, solo practitioners, small firms, and limited-license professionals could serve more people through automation, yet face especially acute financing, expertise, time, and implementation barriers. Large firms and corporate legal departments are better positioned to obtain sophisticated AI and technical support, potentially strengthening existing competitive advantages without addressing underserved consumers’ different legal needs. Established large firms nevertheless face expensive legacy-system replacement. Technologists and smaller AI developers face data, computing, talent, and regulatory barriers; ownership reform and supervised experimentation could enable relationships with lawyers. Consumers and society also bear wider consequences if automated systems reproduce inequality or weaken trust in legal institutions.
